title: When to Tell
subtitle: A guide for the most common in-the-moment question in math teaching: should I just tell them, or let them keep working?

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006) · Kapur, productive failure · Hattie, Visible Learning · Sweller, worked-example effect · NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014).

blocks.text: What it is

A decision guide that names **when explicit instruction (telling) is the right move** and when to hold the tell and let students reason — so direct instruction lands when it’s most powerful instead of by default.

This is not an anti-telling tool. Clear, well-timed direct instruction is one of the highest-impact things a teacher does. The point is that **telling isn’t the enemy — mistimed telling is.** Direct instruction is a *mode* you move into at the right moments, not a phase that fills the first 30 minutes.

**Don’t tell students what they can productively figure out. Do tell them what they can’t reasonably derive — conventions, notation, vocabulary — or what they’ve struggled enough to be ready to receive.**
The two modes
Skilled teaching moves fluidly between two modes, sometimes within the same ten minutes:
Inquiry mode

items: Students reason and struggle through a problem
The teacher questions, monitors, and waits
Best for ideas students can build themselves

blocks.text: Explicit mode

items: The teacher tells, models, names, formalizes
Brief, clear, checked for understanding
Best for conventions — and for consolidation

blocks.text: The art is knowing which mode the moment calls for. That’s what the companion Decision Guide lays out.
What it develops

blocks.label: Effective Teaching Practices
items: Support productive struggle
Build fluency from conceptual understanding
Pose purposeful questions
Elicit & use evidence of thinking

blocks.text: What this is — and isn’t

yes.title: What good timing looks like
items: Telling conventions and notation directly — no struggle needed
Letting students grapple with ideas they can derive
Stepping in when struggle turns unproductive
Formalizing the math *after* students have grappled
Brief, clear explanation broken up with student thinking

no.title: What it is NOT
items: “Never tell” / pure discovery — that fails students
“Always tell first” for ideas they could discover
A 30–40 minute monologue before students do anything
Rescuing students the instant they get stuck
Telling before you’ve seen their thinking

blocks.text: The most common timing error is jumping in too soon — telling students the very thing they were about to figure out. It feels helpful and it quietly teaches students that if they wait, the teacher will do the thinking for them. When students are *productively* stuck (engaged and trying things), that struggle is the learning — protect it.
Why this is on solid research ground

items: **Pure discovery fails** (Kirschner, Sweller & Clark, 2006) — minimal guidance does not work, so we are not anti-telling.
**But struggle-before-instruction wins** for conceptual learning (Kapur, “productive failure”) — so we re-time the tell rather than removing it.
**Teacher Clarity and Direct Instruction are high-impact** in Hattie’s research synthesis — clear, brief, well-timed explanation is a core skill, not a fallback.
**The worked-example effect** — once a concept is understood, explicitly modeling a procedure efficiently builds fluency.

sections.label: Decision guide
sections.sources: Sources: Kapur, productive failure · Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006) · Hattie, Visible Learning · NCTM, Principles to Actions — support productive struggle (2014).

blocks.text: The core decision
TELL when…

items: It’s a **convention, notation, vocabulary, or name** — arbitrary, can’t be derived (e.g., the word *numerator*, the ≤ symbol, “we call this slope”).
Productive struggle has tipped into **unproductive** struggle (see below) — scaffold or model.
Students have **grappled and are ready to formalize** — this is the consolidation, the most powerful tell of all.
A **worked example** will efficiently build a procedure students now understand conceptually.
**Access requires it** — brief pre-teaching of a word or tool for some students.

blocks.text: HOLD the tell when…

items: The idea is **derivable** with reasonable support — ask a question instead.
You’d be **stealing the struggle** — the grappling *is* the point.
Students are **productively stuck** — engaged and trying things (that’s the good kind).
You **haven’t seen their thinking yet** — find out before you decide.
One more minute, a hint, or a peer’s idea would get them there.

blocks.text: Reading the struggle: productive vs. unproductive
The hardest call is the in-the-moment one. Use these signs:

rows: Frustration turning into giving up or acting out
Stuck on access (a word, the task, a tool) — not the math

blocks.text: The sequencing decision (before the lesson)
“When to tell” also applies to the *whole lesson’s* shape — and it depends on the content:

items: **Task before tell** — the default for *conceptual* goals. Let students grapple first, then formalize. (Why a common denominator works; what makes a relationship proportional.)
**Tell, then practice** — appropriate for *convention-heavy* content students can’t derive. (Scientific-notation format; geometry vocabulary; order-of-operations naming.)

blocks.text: Task-before-tell is the default, not a rule. The teacher’s judgment about which the content calls for *is* the skill.
Worked examples from 6–8

rows: That we write `3/4`, and that the bottom is the “denominator”
That you need same-size pieces to add fractions — let the `1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5` error surface it
The notation for scientific notation, e.g. `3.2 × 10⁴`
Why moving the decimal works — let them notice the pattern
That the constant rate of change is called *slope*
That a proportional relationship has a constant ratio — let them find it in a table
Whether two expressions are equivalent — let them test and argue

blocks.title: How to step in without stealing the struggle

blocks.text: When you decide to help, escalate gently — don’t jump straight to the answer:

items: **Ask first:** “What have you tried? Where did it get tricky?”
**Hint, don’t tell:** “What if you drew it?” / “Is it bigger or smaller than 1?”
**Point to a tool or a peer:** “How did that group start?”
**Then, if needed, model** — briefly, and hand the thinking back: “Now you try the next one.”

blocks.text: In the **opener**, most tells are quick (a convention, a name). In **Core Instruction**, the big tell is the consolidation — formalizing the math from student work — plus small mid-task rescues. In **practice**, you tell by re-teaching based on what the evidence shows. Same principle, every component.
